Pregnancy

Hepatitis C in pregnancy: transmission and a child’s follow-up

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A parent’s hepatitis C result does not mean their baby is infected. A clear testing and follow-up plan can separate exposure from infection and connect a child who needs treatment with effective care, without restricting ordinary affection.

Exposure is different from infection

Hepatitis C virus (HCV) can pass from a pregnant person with current infection to their baby during pregnancy or birth. Detectable HCV RNA indicates current infection; an antibody result alone may reflect a previous infection that has cleared.

An exposed baby needs the appropriate test even when well. Some infected children later clear the virus without treatment, but it is inaccurate to assume that the fetus usually clears it or that a healthy appearance rules out infection.

How likely is transmission, and when does it happen?

CDC estimates that roughly 6–7% of perinatally exposed infants acquire HCV. This is a population estimate, not a prediction for one family. Risk is higher with poorly controlled HIV coinfection; effective HIV care matters. A specific HCV RNA level or genotype cannot provide a reliable individual transmission threshold.

Transmission can occur before birth as well as around delivery; it cannot simply be assigned to contact with blood at birth. Discuss current infection, HIV care and any injecting-related exposure confidentially with the team. Risk assessment should support care, never blame.

Pregnancy and delivery planning

When possible, assess and cure HCV before pregnancy. During pregnancy, the team checks HCV RNA and liver health and considers other infections and obstetric needs. There is no routine HCV intervention proven to guarantee prevention of transmission.

Cesarean birth is not recommended solely to prevent HCV. Clinicians generally avoid unnecessary internal fetal monitoring and early artificial rupture of membranes, while responding to actual obstetric needs. New itching or jaundice deserves maternity assessment rather than being assumed to be ordinary HCV.

What if the father or sperm-producing partner has HCV?

A partner’s HCV result does not establish infection in a fetus. However, semen and fertility treatment should not be declared universally risk-free. The couple’s infection status, possible sexual or blood exposure and the clinic’s handling procedures all matter.

Tell the fertility team before insemination, IVF or other treatment. Specialist counselling, testing and cure before conception or fertility treatment when feasible can reduce risk. Do not attempt sperm processing at home or assume that IVF itself prevents every transmission route.

Sexual transmission is possible but uncommon

HCV is mainly blood-borne. Sexual transmission is relatively inefficient, but risk changes with exposure to blood, HIV, other sexually transmitted infections and sexual practices or multiple partners. An old percentage of cases attributed to sex is not a personal risk estimate.

Discuss partner testing and protection without stigma. A long-term mutually monogamous couple does not automatically need to change every sexual practice because of HCV; new or multiple partners, HIV or STI risks require tailored advice, including condoms where appropriate. Avoid sharing blood-contaminated equipment.

Testing an exposed infant

Under the US CDC pathway, infants exposed during pregnancy or birth have an HCV RNA nucleic acid test at age 2–6 months. A detectable result needs a clinician experienced in pediatric HCV. An undetectable result at or after 2 months usually needs no further HCV follow-up unless clinically warranted.

If testing was missed, age 7–17 months calls for an RNA test; at 18 months or older, an antibody test with reflex RNA testing if reactive. Maternal antibodies can confuse earlier antibody results. Local pathways may differ: record the planned test, age and who will explain it, rather than ordering repeated tests yourself.

A positive result needs a care plan

The specialist checks whether infection is current and follows the child’s growth, liver biochemistry and overall health. Liver tests are generally assessed at diagnosis and at least annually, with other investigations guided by the situation. A viral-load number alone does not measure liver damage.

Selected noninvasive assessment or other tests may help evaluate severity. Genotype testing depends on the treatment plan; modern options cover several genotypes, so not every child needs an identical genotype-driven workup. A positive result is not a reason to exclude a child from school or ordinary activities.

Vaccines protect against other infections

There is no HCV vaccine. Children with HCV should receive their routine vaccines and hepatitis A and B vaccination if not immune, according to their local schedule and clinical circumstances. These vaccines protect against other viruses, not against HCV itself.

Age-appropriate influenza vaccination is also important. In CDC guidance it starts at 6 months, with the number of initial doses depending on age and vaccine history. Do not assume a newborn can receive every vaccine or invent an extra dose schedule without the child’s team.

Can infection clear on its own?

Some children clear HCV spontaneously during early childhood. Estimates vary by study and follow-up; newer analyses suggest more clearance than older fixed figures implied. This cannot predict whether an individual child will clear infection.

Follow the testing plan and confirm current HCV RNA before treatment. Possible spontaneous clearance is not a rule to postpone approved treatment until age 7. A specialist balances the child’s current infection, age, liver health and access to effective treatment.

Effective childhood treatment is available

Approved direct-acting antiviral (DAA) treatment is recommended for children with chronic HCV aged 3 years and older, regardless of disease severity. A child younger than 3 or with advanced disease needs specialist assessment; do not infer a routine unapproved early-treatment regimen.

The exact medicine, formulation, duration and checks depend on age, weight, liver status, interactions and local approval. Modern treatment can cure HCV, but not every child follows one 12-week course or has the same result. Taste, vomiting, missed doses and adverse effects need practical support; never repeat or change doses without advice.

Treatment for the pregnant or breastfeeding parent

Current specialist guidance allows individual discussion of DAA treatment during pregnancy, but evidence is limited and DAAs are not routinely recommended solely to prevent transmission. Product-specific warnings matter; ribavirin has particular pregnancy risks. Do not start or stop treatment independently.

After birth, the parent’s RNA should be reassessed. Breastfeeding does not automatically require delaying every DAA until weaning: advice depends on the exact medicine and infant, and lactation evidence is limited. Arrange a liver-care and feeding plan rather than assuming all drugs are interchangeable or proven safe.

Breastfeeding and everyday affection

HCV is not documented to spread through breast milk. Cracked or bleeding nipples require a temporary feeding plan and lactation help to avoid blood exposure; the team may advise expressing and discarding affected milk until healed and using suitable alternative milk. HIV coinfection needs its own specialist feeding plan.

Hugging, holding and ordinary kisses do not transmit HCV. Cover bleeding wounds and prevent another person’s blood from entering broken skin or mucous membranes. Do not share toothbrushes, razors or items that may carry blood. A parent’s diagnosis does not make their touch or ordinary family life unsafe.

Long-term health and keeping appointments

Many infected children have few symptoms and slow disease progression, but serious liver disease can occur. Neither an old percentage of mild disease by age 18 nor a normal-looking child guarantees the outcome. Ongoing assessment and curative treatment improve the care options.

Keep the parent’s and child’s records separate: exposure, actual test dates and results, current infection, vaccination status and medication plan. Tell a new clinician about previous exposure even if appointments were missed. After cure, antibodies can remain positive; blood exposure can cause a new infection.

When a baby or child needs urgent help

Seek urgent assessment for new or worsening jaundice, dark urine or pale stools; do not assume these are HCV. Jaundice in the first 24 hours needs emergency assessment. A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or more needs immediate emergency assessment without waiting for an HCV appointment.

Get emergency help now for breathing difficulty, blue/grey colour or unusual pallor, cold clammy skin, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, a seizure or a seriously unwell child. Jaundice with poor feeding, sleepiness or abnormal movements is also an emergency. Do not wait for all signs or a test result, and do not drive yourself in an emergency.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Before leaving maternity care, ask who will arrange the baby’s age-based HCV test and explain the result; keep the contact and appointment details.

If RNA is detected, attend pediatric specialist follow-up, review vaccines and discuss approved treatment when age-eligible; do not wait for symptoms or stop care because the child looks well.

Agree a separate plan for the parent’s HCV treatment and the baby’s feeding, tell clinicians the exact medicines and get help for blood exposure or nipple injury. Urgent symptoms override a routine test appointment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record parent and child appointments, the planned test and age, results, vaccines, medicines and questions for the team. It cannot interpret RNA or antibodies, estimate a baby’s individual risk, diagnose liver disease or choose treatment and feeding medicines. Recording must never delay urgent help.

When to seek help

Get emergency help for a child with breathing difficulty, blue/grey colour or unusual pallor, cold clammy skin, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, seizure or serious illness. Jaundice before 24 hours, or with poor feeding or sleepiness, also needs emergency assessment. Do not wait for every sign or self-drive. Later new or worsening jaundice needs urgent assessment. Fever of 38°C or more in a baby under 3 months needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not change antiviral or feeding plans without appropriate advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Exposure does not establish infection: arrange the correct age-based infant test.
  • Transmission can occur during pregnancy or birth; individual risk is not a fixed percentage or RNA threshold.
  • Confirmed childhood infection needs specialist follow-up and approved treatment from age 3, not automatic waiting until age 7.
  • Vaccines protect against other infections; no HCV vaccine is available.
  • Ordinary affection is safe. Blood exposure, feeding injuries and exact medicines need practical, individualized advice.

Frequently asked questions

Can HCV pass to a baby during pregnancy?

Yes, during pregnancy or birth when the pregnant parent has current infection. Exposure is not the same as infection; testing is needed even if the baby seems well.

What is the chance?

CDC estimates roughly 6–7% among perinatally exposed infants, with higher risk in poorly controlled HIV coinfection. These group figures and RNA results cannot give an exact personal prediction.

Can a father’s infection infect the fetus through sperm?

His result alone does not diagnose fetal infection. Partner exposure and fertility-clinic precautions still matter; testing, counselling and treatment before conception when feasible are safer than assuming semen or IVF is universally risk-free.

Which test does an exposed baby need?

The US CDC recommends HCV RNA at 2–6 months. Missed tests have age-based catch-up pathways; antibody testing before 18 months can reflect maternal antibodies. Ask the team to document and explain the child’s results.

Should treatment wait for spontaneous clearance?

Some children clear infection, but not predictably. Confirm current RNA and discuss approved DAA treatment from age 3; possible clearance is not a routine instruction to wait until age 7.

Is there a vaccine, and are antivirals always successful?

There is no HCV vaccine. Keep routine and indicated hepatitis A/B and age-appropriate flu vaccines up to date. Antivirals can cure HCV, but formulation, adherence, interactions and follow-up matter; no individual cure is guaranteed.

Can we breastfeed, hold and kiss the baby?

Ordinary affection is safe, and HCV is not documented to spread through milk. Get a temporary plan for cracked or bleeding nipples, prevent blood exposure and check any HIV or exact medication-related feeding advice.

Which symptoms should not wait for an HCV visit?

Breathing difficulty, abnormal blue/grey or unusually pale colour, cold clammy skin, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, seizure or serious illness needs emergency help now. Jaundice in the first 24 hours, or with poor feeding or sleepiness, is also an emergency. Later new or worsening jaundice needs urgent assessment. A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or more needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not self-drive or wait for every sign.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
